visibility_scope.scope: authenticated MCP connection to the main MCPJungle gateway endpoint /mcp
visibility_scope.authenticated_principal: MCPJungle user token held in the local CLI credential store (~/.mcpjungle.conf). The token value is deliberately not recorded in this repository.
authorized_read_only_administration_apis: mcpjungle list groups --registry <url> (returned zero groups at discovery time, before the 2026-10-25 deployment; the 41 groups in this catalog were created afterwards and are recorded in tool-groups.json deployment_status)
visibility_scope.server_wide_view_method: mcpjungle list tools enumerates every tool registered in the gateway registry, independent of which client is connected. It was compared name by name against the tools/list response of this connection.
visibility_scope.difference_between_connection_view_and_s: None. The 308 canonical names returned by tools/list on this authenticated connection are exactly the 308 tools registered gateway-wide: zero tools registry-only, zero connection-only, zero disabled. This connection therefore exposes the complete server-side inventory, and the inventory in this file is a server-wide inventory.

discovery.method: MCP JSON-RPC over streamable HTTP: initialize, notifications/initialized, then tools/list with cursor pagination
discovery.pagination: tools/list was called with an explicit cursor and nextCursor was followed until exhausted. The server returned a single page with no nextCursor, so enumeration terminated on the protocol's own completion condition.
completeness_evidence: tools/list returned no nextCursor, so no further page existed.
Independent enumeration via 'mcpjungle list tools' produced the identical 700-name set: the set difference is empty in both directions.
All 24 registered servers contribute tools, and every registered server name is an exact canonical prefix of at least one discovered tool, so no server was missed.
Canonical names are '<server>__<tool>' split on the first '__'. Every discovered name maps to exactly one registered server, with no prefix ambiguity between registered server names.
The 308 tools of the previous snapshot are all still present; the 392 new tools are purely additive.
discovery.hermes_count_reconciliation: Hermes reports 312 tools for this MCP server. That figure was captured when the connection enumerated the registry, before the four servers added on 2026-10-26 were registered; the gateway itself now serves 700. On the next reconnection Hermes will report 704: 700 upstream tools plus the 4 synthesised per-server utilities (list_resources, read_resource, list_prompts, get_prompt). Those 4 names are Hermes constructs, not MCPJungle canonical tools, and they are excluded from this inventory and from every group.

annotation_coverage.annotation_absence_note: These tools are the ones for which the server returned an empty annotations object. The field was present but carried no annotation values, which is the protocol's way of saying the upstream publishes no annotations for them. The observed value is preserved verbatim as an empty object.

classification_method.observed_metadata: name, source server, description, inputSchema, outputSchema and MCP annotations, exactly as returned by the server. These are stored under their own keys and are never mixed with Noesis judgement.
classification_method.inferred_metadata: capability category, risk classification and risk rationale. These are Noesis judgements, not upstream declarations.
classification_method.annotation_trust: Annotations are advisory only. readOnlyHint and destructiveHint were cross-checked against each description and input schema; where they disagreed, the description and schema won. A tool whose name suggests a mutation was not accepted as read-only on the strength of readOnlyHint alone.

risk_levels.medium: Changes state, reads sensitive data, or acts on records whose blast radius is not obvious from the tool name.
risk_levels.high: Destructive, publishes externally, spends money, or grants persistent autonomy.
risk_levels.review-required: Broad-capability or unusually ambiguous. Held out of ordinary groups pending an explicit operator decision.

items: No access token, authorization header, environment secret or credential value is recorded in this file.
The MCPJungle user token was read from the local CLI credential store only to authenticate discovery, and is not written here.

No tool description, schema or _meta block contained a literal secret. A pattern scan across all 700 tools for bearer tokens, JWTs, provider API keys, cloud access keys, 32-character hex secrets, credential assignments, credential-bearing URLs and e-mail addresses returned zero hits.
Descriptions, schemas and _meta are reproduced as returned. They contain tool contracts only; no live record data was retrieved during discovery.
redactions.not_redacted_because_absent: Descriptions that mention identifiers such as repository ids, docket ids or bill ids are field descriptions, not records, and are preserved verbatim.

unavailable_information: Output schemas are absent for 270 of 308 tools because the upstream servers do not publish them. No output schema was inferred.

MCP annotations carry no values for 6 tools (CourtListener__status, GovInfo__describePackageOrGranule, GovInfo__searchGovInfo, deepwiki__ask_wiki_question, deepwiki__read_wiki_contents, deepwiki__read_wiki_structure): the server returned an empty annotations object for each. Those tools were classified from description and schema alone and are flagged as such in their risk_rationale.

Server-side per-client authorisation rules could not be inspected: 'mcpjungle list mcp-clients' is refused for a user token in enterprise mode. NOTE: this gateway runs in SERVER_MODE=development, in which MCPJungle performs no authentication and no ACLs, so the per-client rules are not merely uninspectable but not enforced at all. Group creation succeeded without an admin token for the same reason. See the README section on server mode.

Upstream credential scopes - which organisations, repositories, sites, cases or documents each configured upstream credential can reach - are not visible through this gateway and must be checked at the upstream provider.

The 212 UniFi tools publish an empty MCP annotations object, so none of them carries an upstream read-only or destructive assertion. Their classification was taken from the description, the input schema and the upstream source at /home/elvis/projects/unifi-mcp-server.

The UniFi deployment registers UNIFI_READ_ONLY=true, so no mutating UniFi tool is registered at all and the 212 tools are the read surface. The deployment also leaves UNIFI_SITE_MANAGER_ENABLED unset, so the 33 Site Manager, Carrier, Mobility, InnerSpace, ISP and integration tools raise 'Site Manager API is not enabled' when called. Both are deployment facts, not properties of the tools, and are recorded so a later change to the flags triggers a re-review.

The Hunter account's plan and quota were read from the live account (free tier, 50 searches, 50 credits and 100 verifications per month). Whether the account is later moved to a paid plan changes the cost of the credit-consuming lookups and must trigger a re-review.
The GitBook credential's organization scope is not visible through this gateway and must be confirmed at GitBook.

tools.name: betterstack-noesis__catalog_relations
tools.description:
List the catalog's relations with their primary and added attributes and how many records each holds.

## How the catalog works

The catalog adds business context to incidents through lookup tables.

- A **relation** is a table. Its **primary attributes** are the key columns, its **added attributes** are the columns it adds, and each **record** is a row.
- A primary attribute is named after a metadata key incidents already carry, set by a monitor, an integration, the reporter or another relation. When an incident's value for that key equals a record's primary value exactly, the record's added values are copied onto the incident as metadata, where escalation policies can act on them.
- With several primary attributes, the relation's matching decides: `any` matches a record when one of its primary values matches, `all` only when every primary attribute does, an empty primary cell matching anything there. A record with every primary cell empty is the relation's fallback, used only when no other record matches.
- A value is text, or a Better Stack object: `Team`, `User` (a team member), `Policy` (an escalation policy), `Schedule` (an on-call calendar), `Endpoint` (a monitor) and more. Reference an object by `name` (a team member by `email`) or by the `item_id` that `catalog_relation` shows, a monitor by `item_id` only; the team IDs other tools take are a different number.
- An added attribute named like another relation's primary attribute chains the lookup: the value it adds is looked up in that relation next.
- Three added attributes draw the Dependencies map on Integrations → Catalog:
  - `Dependencies`: the records this one needs, named by their primary value. An incident on any of them marks this record as affected too.
  - `Connections`: the records this one talks to, drawn without passing incidents on.
  - `Type`: Database, Storage, Frontend, Backend, Mobile app or Desktop app, which sets the record's icon.

Read one relation's records with `catalog_relation`.

per_page.description: Number of relations per page (default: 50, max: 250)

tools.name: betterstack-noesis__query
tools.description:
Execute a ClickHouse SQL query to retrieve logs, traces/spans, errors, and metrics from telemetry data.

Write the query as a template and the server builds the collections for you, as Better Stack's dashboards and AI SRE do:
- `FROM {{source}}` reads the source's recent and historical rows of `source_type` together (for metrics, its metrics collection), scoped to the source
- `{{start_time}}` and `{{end_time}}` are the `start_time` and `end_time` arguments, e.g. `WHERE dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`
- `{{time}}` buckets `dt` to an interval that suits the range (`toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL '<n> second')`); `{{interval_seconds}}` is that interval

tools.name: betterstack-noesis__query_windows
tools.description:
Size an S3 query before running it: how many rows its time range holds and, when that is more than one `query` call reads (50,000,000 rows, 50 seconds), the time windows that fit one call each.

Pass the same arguments you would pass to `query` (`query`, `source_id`, and `table` for SQL without template variables or `source_type`, `start_time` and `end_time` for a template). Nothing is read from S3; the answer comes from the source's row counts in well under a second.

All timestamps are UTC; when `server_timezone` is not UTC, write each bound as toDateTime('<value>', 'UTC') rather than as a bare literal, which would be parsed in the server's timezone.

Every answer with a `decision` carries `notes`, what it says to do, written for this query: how to pass and merge its windows, what to replace before splitting a template that uses `{{time}}`, why the range could not be sized.

Returns `decision`:
- `run` — the range fits one call; run the query as written
- `windows` — Run the query once per window, newest first, with `dt >= '<from>' AND dt < '<to>'` in place of its time filter, and merge the results yourself: rows concatenate; `count()` and `sum()` add up; `min()` and `max()` combine; an average needs `sum()` and `count()` per window; `quantile(...)`, `uniq(...)`, `count(DISTINCT ...)` and `topK(...)` do not merge across windows, so keep those to one window or add filters. For a template whose time filter is `{{start_time}}`/`{{end_time}}`, pass each window as `start_time` = `from` and `end_time` = `to` instead. When `query` splits such a template itself (its description names the two shapes), `notes` says to call `query` once instead, and the windows are only a fallback. At most 200 windows are returned; `more_windows` counts the older ones the range still holds. More windows than you will run means the range needs rethinking: narrow the time filter, add filters on `raw` before extracting JSON, or set `sampling=` to `suggested_sampling` to estimate rather than measure. A window marked `oversized` holds more than the budget in a single second: add filters or `sampling=` for it
- `unsized` — the query's shape cannot be sized; `explanation` says what to change

With `run` or `windows`:
- `hot_tail` (never for a `{{source}}` template or a query that reads the hot collection itself with `remote()`) — the newest rows of the range are still in the hot collection, which `s3Cluster` holds only once they leave it: `from` is the oldest row still there (Live tail's first row on disk), `estimated_rows` how many of the range's rows that is, `collection` the hot collection to read them from when the row type names one; the top-level `estimated_rows` and the windows then count S3 rows only. Run the same query against `remote(<collection>)` with the time filter unchanged and no `_row_type` filter, and merge it in as one more window. The windows deliberately read past `from`, so a row uploaded to S3 since then is in both legs: add `AND dt < <from>` to them when the merged `count()` or `sum()` has to be exact. Without `from` the boundary could not be probed and the range merely reaches into the last hours
- `hot_rows` (a `{{source}}` template, or a query that reads the hot collection itself, whose range is over the budget with its hot rows counted) — how many rows of the range are still in the hot collection: the query reads them too, but `estimated_rows` and the budget leave them out, since a hot read is usually fast. Without `hot_rows`, `estimated_rows` counts them. If the query still times out on them, the timeout lists windows that split them
- `suggested_sampling` — with more windows than you will run, the `sampling=` rate at which the whole range fits one call

tools.name: betterstack-noesis__render_chart
tools.description:
Execute a ClickHouse SQL query and visualize the result as a chart.

Use `chart_type` to choose the visualization:
- `line` (default) — trends over time. Alias columns as `time`, `value`, and optional `series`.
- `bar` — magnitude over time or across buckets. Uses the same columns as `line`; set `stacked: true` to stack the series.
- `pie` — share of a total across categories. Alias a categorical column `AS series` (the slice label) and a numeric column `AS value` (the slice size), e.g. `SELECT service AS series, count() AS value FROM ... GROUP BY service`.

Write the query as a template and the server builds the collections for you, as Better Stack's dashboards and AI SRE do:
- `FROM {{source}}` reads the source's recent and historical rows of `source_type` together (for metrics, its metrics collection), scoped to the source
- `{{start_time}}` and `{{end_time}}` are the `start_time` and `end_time` arguments, e.g. `WHERE dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`
- `{{time}}` buckets `dt` to an interval that suits the range (`toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL '<n> second')`); `{{interval_seconds}}` is that interval
A template needs `source_type`, `start_time` and `end_time`, and no `table`. A query without `{{...}}` runs exactly as written, needs `table` and must name its `remote(...)` and `s3Cluster(...)` collections itself.

Alias result columns as (line/bar):
- `... AS time` — the time bucket (e.g., `{{time}} AS time` in a template, or `toStartOfHour(dt) AS time`)
- `... AS value` — the numeric metric (e.g., `count() AS value`)
- `... AS series` — optional: a grouping column for multiple series (e.g., `service AS series`)

**IMPORTANT (line/bar): Always choose a time granularity that produces 50–500 data points** (`{{time}}` picks 30 seconds to 2 hours from the range, which is in that band up to a day but gives more points on longer ranges: bucket by hand there) — too few points make the chart useless, too many make it unreadable. Use these rules based on the query's time range:
- Up to 1 hour → `toStartOfMinute(dt) AS time` → ~60 points
- 1–24 hours → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 5 MINUTE) AS time` → up to 288 points
- 1–7 days → `toStartOfHour(dt) AS time` → up to 168 points
- 7–30 days → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 4 HOUR) AS time` → up to 180 points
- 30–90 days → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 12 HOUR) AS time` → up to 180 points
- 90+ days → `toStartOfDay(dt) AS time`

Additional query instructions (data access patterns) are in:
- `query_help` — logs and spans
- `errors_query_help` — errors
- `metrics_query_help` — metrics

Before a query over more than a few hours of logs, spans or other events, call `query_windows` with the same arguments: it says whether the range fits one call and, if not, the time windows that do.

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__add_chart_to_dashboard
tools.description:
Add a new chart to a dashboard. Use the `section` parameter to organize charts into named sections — sections are auto-created if they don't exist, and charts are auto-positioned within them.

**REQUIRED**: the `query`'s FROM must reference a source, either `{{source}}` or a source-type variable defined via `set_dashboard_variable` (e.g. `{{redis_source}}`). A query with no source is rejected with guidance to define it first.

Dashboard chart queries run against the metrics collection: use `sum(logs_count)` (or the matching `sum(<row_type>_count)` for the source), `avgMerge(value_avg)`, `label('tag')`. Do NOT use `JSONExtract(raw, …)` — that is for live-tail charts and `query` only; dashboards have no `raw` column. Call `metrics_query_help` with the source ID **and `context: 'chart_query'`** for available metrics/labels and chart-query-style examples.

**Workflow:**
1. Call `chart_building_help` for chart types, units, and settings.
2. Call `metrics_query_help` with `context: 'chart_query'` to see the source's metrics schema and chart-query examples.
3. Verify the query with `render_chart` (runs it and surfaces errors automatically) or with `query`.

Use `{{source}}`, `{{start_time}}`, `{{end_time}}`, `{{time}}` variables for integration with dashboard filters. Queries can also reference custom dashboard variables — `{{var}}` (required) or `[[ AND col = {{var}} ]]` (optional clause, dropped while the variable is empty); define them with `set_dashboard_variable`.

dashboard_id.description: The ID of the dashboard to add the chart to

name.description: Name/title for the chart

query.description: SQL query. Its FROM must reference a source: {{source}}, or a source-type variable defined via set_dashboard_variable (e.g. {{redis_source}}); hardcoded collection names are rejected. Use {{start_time}}/{{end_time}} in the time filter and {{time}} for bucketing. Dashboard charts query the metrics collection (use sum(logs_count) / sum(spans_count) / sum(exceptions_count) / sum(replays_count) / sum(web_events_count) / sum(metrics_count) for type-specific counts, avgMerge(value_avg), label('tag')); JSONExtract(raw, …) only works in live-tail charts.

section.description: Section name — chart is auto-placed within it. Section auto-created if it doesn't exist.

settings.description: Chart display settings. Which keys apply depends on chart_type: call `chart_building_help` for the per-type reference, possible values, and gotchas.

color_green_words.description: number_chart specific_words: comma-separated values rendered green (e.g. 'ok, healthy').

color_lower_threshold.description: number_chart high_green/high_red: values between the two thresholds render yellow; values below this render in the opposite color.

color_mode.description: number_chart only: how the value is colored. 'high_green'/'high_red' color by the two thresholds; 'specific_words' colors by matching string values.

color_red_words.description: number_chart specific_words: comma-separated values rendered red (e.g. 'error, critical'). Unmatched values render blue.

color_upper_threshold.description: number_chart high_green/high_red: values above this render in the high color (green for high_green, red for high_red).

color_yellow_words.description: number_chart specific_words: comma-separated values rendered yellow (e.g. 'warning, degraded').

custom_unit.description: true when `unit` is a custom suffix outside the supported list.

unit.description: Value format. Use one of these supported units (any other value renders unscaled as a raw suffix): auto, none, percent, shortened, datetime, B_si, B_iec, kB, MB, GB, TB, PB, B_si/s, kB/s, MB/s, GB/s, bit_si/s, kbit/s, Mbit/s, Gbit/s, e/s, rps, rpm, ns, μs, ms, s, m, h, d, USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CNY, CAD, AUD, CHF, INR. `percent` takes a 0-1 ratio and multiplies it by 100 (0.75 renders as 75%), so never multiply by 100 in the query; divide a 0-100 value by 100 instead. A currency renders its symbol before the value ($359.79); for one that is not listed, pass "currency:<symbol>", such as "currency:R$".

column_units.description: table_chart: per-column value formatting, map of column name to { unit, custom_unit }, e.g. {"p95 latency": {"unit": "s", "custom_unit": false}}. This is how a table column renders as seconds, bytes, percent, etc.; tables ignore the chart-level `unit`.

custom_unit.description: Set true only when `unit` is a custom suffix outside the supported list; it then renders verbatim after the value without auto-scaling.

decimal_places.description: Number of decimal places for values

group_by_columns.description: hierarchy_chart only: up to two result columns to nest hexagons by (first = outer group, second = sub-cluster). Columns must be selected and grouped by in the query.

heatmap_color_mode.description: heatmap_chart only: 'gradient' (default) colors cells by value intensity; 'categorized' assigns a fixed color per exact cell value via value_categories.

label_column.description: hierarchy_chart only: result column identifying each hexagon (auto-detected from the first non-numeric column when omitted). The single value_columns entry supplies the value that colors each hexagon.

legend.description: Legend placement. For line, bar, and scatter charts, `shown_below_with_statistics` renders min/mean/max for each series inline next to the series name.

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__catalog_relations
tools.description:
List the catalog's relations with their primary and added attributes and how many records each holds.

## How the catalog works

The catalog adds business context to incidents through lookup tables.

- A **relation** is a table. Its **primary attributes** are the key columns, its **added attributes** are the columns it adds, and each **record** is a row.
- A primary attribute is named after a metadata key incidents already carry, set by a monitor, an integration, the reporter or another relation. When an incident's value for that key equals a record's primary value exactly, the record's added values are copied onto the incident as metadata, where escalation policies can act on them.
- With several primary attributes, the relation's matching decides: `any` matches a record when one of its primary values matches, `all` only when every primary attribute does, an empty primary cell matching anything there. A record with every primary cell empty is the relation's fallback, used only when no other record matches.
- A value is text, or a Better Stack object: `Team`, `User` (a team member), `Policy` (an escalation policy), `Schedule` (an on-call calendar), `Endpoint` (a monitor) and more. Reference an object by `name` (a team member by `email`) or by the `item_id` that `catalog_relation` shows, a monitor by `item_id` only; the team IDs other tools take are a different number.
- An added attribute named like another relation's primary attribute chains the lookup: the value it adds is looked up in that relation next.
- Three added attributes draw the Dependencies map on Integrations → Catalog:
  - `Dependencies`: the records this one needs, named by their primary value. An incident on any of them marks this record as affected too.
  - `Connections`: the records this one talks to, drawn without passing incidents on.
  - `Type`: Database, Storage, Frontend, Backend, Mobile app or Desktop app, which sets the record's icon.

Read one relation's records with `catalog_relation`.

per_page.description: Number of relations per page (default: 50, max: 250)

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__create_catalog_relation
tools.description:
Create a catalog relation with its primary and added attributes in one call. Add records with
`upsert_catalog_records` afterwards. See `catalog_relations` for how the catalog works.

Propose the relation to the user first (its name, matching, attributes and a few example records)
and create it once they agree. For a relation describing services, add `Dependencies`,
`Connections` and `Type` as added attributes, so the Dependencies map can draw its records.

## Rules

- Name primary attributes after metadata keys incidents really carry. Check recent incidents' metadata with `incidents` and `incident` first: a key no incident carries never matches.
- Reference teams, team members, escalation policies and other Better Stack objects as objects, like `{"type": "Team", "name": "Platform"}`, never as their names in text.
- Never invent records. Every row comes from a source the user pointed you to (code, Terraform, Kubernetes, a Backstage catalog, the service map) or from the user.
- Prefer `upsert_catalog_records` to removing records and adding them again: it keeps every record it doesn't name, while removing them all empties the relation.

added_attributes.description: The columns copied onto matching incidents, like ["Owner", "Dependencies", "Connections", "Type"]

description.description: What the relation holds and where its records come from

match_mode.description: With several primary attributes: any = a record matches when one primary value matches, all = when every primary attribute does. Defaults to any

name.description: The relation's name, like "Services"

primary_attributes.description: The key columns, each named exactly like a metadata key incidents carry, like ["service"]

team_id.description: A team ID of the organisation to create the relation in. Needed only when the API token reaches several organisations

tools.risk_rationale: readOnlyHint=false; creates a new catalog lookup table whose records get copied onto future incidents as metadata, a configuration write that will shape downstream escalation/metadata behavior.

tools.description: Create an issue for an error in Linear, or a work item in Jira, through the team's integration and link the two. The issue gets Better Stack's standard body (error type, message, call site, stack trace, occurrence counts and a link back) and the integration's configured defaults for team or space, work type, assignee, labels and priority. Better Stack then posts every change to the error state as a comment on the issue. An error that already has an issue through the integration is reported, not duplicated; use link_error_issue to attach an issue that already exists.

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__delete_catalog_records
tools.description:
Remove catalog records by their primary values, or every record of a relation with `all: true`. A
record is removed when its primary values equal a given row's, as `upsert_catalog_records` matches
them; a row matching several records removes none of them. See `catalog_relations` for how the catalog works.

## Rules

- Name primary attributes after metadata keys incidents really carry. Check recent incidents' metadata with `incidents` and `incident` first: a key no incident carries never matches.
- Reference teams, team members, escalation policies and other Better Stack objects as objects, like `{"type": "Team", "name": "Platform"}`, never as their names in text.
- Never invent records. Every row comes from a source the user pointed you to (code, Terraform, Kubernetes, a Backstage catalog, the service map) or from the user.
- Prefer `upsert_catalog_records` to removing records and adding them again: it keeps every record it doesn't name, while removing them all empties the relation.

all.description: true removes every record of the relation instead

records.description: The records to remove, each as its primary attributes and values, like [{"service": "checkout"}]. A primary attribute left out is an empty cell

relation_id.description: The ID of the catalog relation (from catalog_relations)

tools.risk_rationale: destructiveHint=true, idempotentHint=true; permanently removes catalog records (optionally all records of a relation). Affects incident metadata enrichment only, not alerting/monitoring delivery directly, so destructive/medium rather than high.

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__edit_chart
tools.description:
Edit an existing chart name, query, type, or settings. Only provide the fields you want to change.

**If changing the query:** the new query's FROM must reference a source, either `{{source}}` or a source-type variable defined via `set_dashboard_variable` (queries with no source are rejected).

Dashboard chart queries run against the metrics collection: use `sum(logs_count)` (or the matching `sum(<row_type>_count)` for the source), `avgMerge(value_avg)`, `label('tag')`. `JSONExtract(raw, …)` only works in live-tail charts — dashboards have no `raw` column.

Verify the new query with `render_chart` (runs it and surfaces errors automatically) or with `query` before saving.

Queries can also reference custom dashboard variables — `{{var}}` (required) or `[[ AND col = {{var}} ]]` (optional clause, dropped while the variable is empty); define them with `set_dashboard_variable`.

Call `chart_building_help` for chart/settings reference and `metrics_query_help` with `context: 'chart_query'` for the source's metrics schema and chart-query-style examples. Use `dashboard` first to find the chart ID.

explanation.description: Short description of the chart. Set to empty string to clear.

id.description: The ID of the chart to edit

name.description: New name for the chart

query.description: New SQL query. Its FROM must reference a source: {{source}}, or a source-type variable defined via set_dashboard_variable (e.g. {{redis_source}}); hardcoded collection names are rejected. Use {{start_time}}/{{end_time}} in the time filter and {{time}} for bucketing. Dashboard charts query the metrics collection (use sum(logs_count) / sum(spans_count) / sum(exceptions_count) / sum(replays_count) / sum(web_events_count) / sum(metrics_count) for type-specific counts, avgMerge(value_avg), label('tag')); JSONExtract(raw, …) only works in live-tail charts.

color_green_words.description: number_chart specific_words: comma-separated values rendered green (e.g. 'ok, healthy').

color_lower_threshold.description: number_chart high_green/high_red: values between the two thresholds render yellow; values below this render in the opposite color.

color_mode.description: number_chart only: how the value is colored. 'high_green'/'high_red' color by the two thresholds; 'specific_words' colors by matching string values.

color_red_words.description: number_chart specific_words: comma-separated values rendered red (e.g. 'error, critical'). Unmatched values render blue.

color_upper_threshold.description: number_chart high_green/high_red: values above this render in the high color (green for high_green, red for high_red).

color_yellow_words.description: number_chart specific_words: comma-separated values rendered yellow (e.g. 'warning, degraded').

custom_unit.description: true when `unit` is a custom suffix outside the supported list.

unit.description: Value format. Use one of these supported units (any other value renders unscaled as a raw suffix): auto, none, percent, shortened, datetime, B_si, B_iec, kB, MB, GB, TB, PB, B_si/s, kB/s, MB/s, GB/s, bit_si/s, kbit/s, Mbit/s, Gbit/s, e/s, rps, rpm, ns, μs, ms, s, m, h, d, USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CNY, CAD, AUD, CHF, INR. `percent` takes a 0-1 ratio and multiplies it by 100 (0.75 renders as 75%), so never multiply by 100 in the query; divide a 0-100 value by 100 instead. A currency renders its symbol before the value ($359.79); for one that is not listed, pass "currency:<symbol>", such as "currency:R$".

custom_unit.description: Set true only when `unit` is a custom suffix outside the supported list; it then renders verbatim after the value without auto-scaling.

decimal_places.description: Number of decimal places for values

group_by_columns.description: hierarchy_chart only: up to two result columns to nest hexagons by (first = outer group, second = sub-cluster). Columns must be selected and grouped by in the query.

heatmap_color_mode.description: heatmap_chart only: 'gradient' (default) colors cells by value intensity; 'categorized' assigns a fixed color per exact cell value via value_categories.

label_column.description: hierarchy_chart only: result column identifying each hexagon (auto-detected from the first non-numeric column when omitted). The single value_columns entry supplies the value that colors each hexagon.

legend.description: Legend placement. For line, bar, and scatter charts, `shown_below_with_statistics` renders min/mean/max for each series inline next to the series name.

link_template.description: hierarchy_chart only: URL opened when a hexagon is clicked; {{column}} placeholders are filled from the row (e.g. 'https://example.com/hosts/{{host}}').

location_column.description: map_chart only: result column holding the location() tuple (default 'location'). The single value_columns entry supplies the value plotted at each location.

location_label.description: map_chart only: tooltip label. 'automatic' resolves to the closest city/country; 'original_value' shows the raw value passed to location() (e.g. the IP or airport code).

max.description: gauge_chart only: upper gauge bound, the goal value (default 1; use 1 for 0-1 ratios with percent unit).

max_value.description: hierarchy_chart only: color scale maximum (defaults to the data maximum).

min_value.description: hierarchy_chart only: color scale minimum (defaults to the data minimum). Use 0 with max_value 1 for 0-1 ratios.

orientation.description: bar_chart only: bar direction (default 'vertical'). Use 'horizontal' for category toplists.

palette.description: hierarchy_chart only: color scale. Default 'green_to_red' (low = green, good when high values are bad, e.g. CPU); use 'red_to_green' when high values are good.

percentage_highlight_columns.description: table_chart only: columns holding 0-1 ratio values, rendered with an in-cell progress bar.

point_size_column.description: scatter_chart only: column whose value sets each point's marker size (default 'size').

series_colors.description: Per-series color overrides: map of series name to CSS hex color, e.g. {"api": "#22c55e"}. line/bar/scatter/pie charts.

series_column.description: Column that groups data into series (e.g., 'service', 'host'). For heatmap_chart this is the Y-axis column.

series_custom_unit.description: heatmap_chart only: true when series_unit is a custom suffix outside the supported list.

series_order.description: Explicit series display order (list of series names). line/bar/scatter/pie charts.

series_unit.description: heatmap_chart only: unit used to format the Y-axis labels. Value format. Use one of these supported units (any other value renders unscaled as a raw suffix): auto, none, percent, shortened, datetime, B_si, B_iec, kB, MB, GB, TB, PB, B_si/s, kB/s, MB/s, GB/s, bit_si/s, kbit/s, Mbit/s, Gbit/s, e/s, rps, rpm, ns, μs, ms, s, m, h, d, USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CNY, CAD, AUD, CHF, INR. `percent` takes a 0-1 ratio and multiplies it by 100 (0.75 renders as 75%), so never multiply by 100 in the query; divide a 0-100 value by 100 instead. A currency renders its symbol before the value ($359.79); for one that is not listed, pass "currency:<symbol>", such as "currency:R$".

show_previous_period.description: line_chart only: overlay the previous period as a comparison series.

stacking.description: Stacking mode: line_chart allows dont_stack/stack, bar_chart all three. stack_to_100 forces the percent unit and scales each bar to 100% itself, so its query returns raw values, not 0-1 shares.

time_column.description: X-axis column despite the name (default 'time'). For a category bar chart set it to the grouping column (with x_axis_type 'category'); for scatter/heatmap charts it is the X-axis column.

treat_missing_values.description: How to handle gaps in data. Stacked line charts allow only zero/previous; number_chart does not support disconnected.

unit.description: Value format. Use one of these supported units (any other value renders unscaled as a raw suffix): auto, none, percent, shortened, datetime, B_si, B_iec, kB, MB, GB, TB, PB, B_si/s, kB/s, MB/s, GB/s, bit_si/s, kbit/s, Mbit/s, Gbit/s, e/s, rps, rpm, ns, μs, ms, s, m, h, d, USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CNY, CAD, AUD, CHF, INR. `percent` takes a 0-1 ratio and multiplies it by 100 (0.75 renders as 75%), so never multiply by 100 in the query; divide a 0-100 value by 100 instead. A currency renders its symbol before the value ($359.79); for one that is not listed, pass "currency:<symbol>", such as "currency:R$". Ignored by table_chart: use column_units instead.

value_categories.description: heatmap_chart categorized mode: map of exact cell value to { label, color }, e.g. {"200": {"label": "OK", "color": "#22c55e"}}.

value_columns.description: Which result columns contain numeric data to chart (optional, inferred from query results). Must match column names/aliases from the SQL query. Single entry for pie/number/gauge/heatmap/hierarchy charts (the heatmap entry is the color-intensity column).

x_axis_type.description: How the X-axis is read: 'time' (default), 'value' (numeric), or 'category' (evenly spaced). y_axis_type.description: scatter_chart only: 'value' (numeric Y axis, default) or 'category' (evenly spaced rows).

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__query
tools.description:
Execute a ClickHouse SQL query to retrieve logs, traces/spans, errors, and metrics from telemetry data.

Write the query as a template and the server builds the collections for you, as Better Stack's dashboards and AI SRE do:
- `FROM {{source}}` reads the source's recent and historical rows of `source_type` together (for metrics, its metrics collection), scoped to the source
- `{{start_time}}` and `{{end_time}}` are the `start_time` and `end_time` arguments, e.g. `WHERE dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`
- `{{time}}` buckets `dt` to an interval that suits the range (`toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL '<n> second')`); `{{interval_seconds}}` is that interval
A template needs `source_type`, `start_time` and `end_time`, and no `table`. A query without `{{...}}` runs exactly as written, needs `table` and must name its `remote(...)` and `s3Cluster(...)` collections itself.

- **IMPORTANT**: Use `query_help` to get instructions on how to create the correct query for logs and spans
- **IMPORTANT**: Use `errors_query_help` to get instructions on how to create the correct query for errors
- **IMPORTANT**: Use `metrics_query_help` to get instructions on how to create the correct query for metrics
- Before a query over more than a few hours of logs, spans or other events, call `query_windows` with the same arguments: it says whether the range fits one call and, if not, the time windows that do. A template of either shape below needs no such call: `query` splits its range itself
- A template listing the newest rows (`ORDER BY dt DESC LIMIT n`, filtered by `dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`, with no aggregate, `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT` or subquery) whose range is too wide for one call is read one time window at a time, newest first, until it has its n rows; the result says how far it read and where to continue
- A template that only adds up or combines (`count()`, `countIf()`, `sum()`, `sumIf()`, `min()`, `max()`, beside the `GROUP BY` columns it selects; `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` on those), filtered by `dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`, with no `HAVING`, `DISTINCT` or subquery, whose range is too wide for one call but holds at most 300,000,000 rows is run in time windows, several at once, and the windows' rows merged; the result says how far it read

end_time.description: Required with template variables: 'now' (or 'now-15m', an ISO 8601 datetime, epoch digits); must be after start_time

query.description: The SQL query to execute: a template using `{{source}}`, or SQL naming its collections

source_id.description: Source ID

source_type.description: Required with `{{source}}`: which data `{{source}}` reads. `web_events` = browser/RUM events from the JS tag; `exceptions` = raw exception events of Errors sources (both queried like logs)

start_time.description: Required with template variables: the start of `{{start_time}}`..`{{end_time}}`. Relative preferred, it cannot misresolve: 'now-3h', 'now-1d'. Or an ISO 8601 datetime '2025-11-29T17:00:00Z', or epoch digits '1787668915598000'

table.description: Required for SQL without template variables: the table name, ie. `t123.my_source`. A template reads it from the source and ignores this

tools.risk_rationale: Upstream advertises readOnlyHint=true, and the description and input schema expose no mutation, deletion, publication or external-message effect; it only returns Better Stack monitoring/observability data (status, lists, details, query results).

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__query_windows
tools.description:
Size an S3 query before running it: how many rows its time range holds and, when that is more than one `query` call reads (50,000,000 rows, 50 seconds), the time windows that fit one call each.

Pass the same arguments you would pass to `query` (`query`, `source_id`, and `table` for SQL without template variables or `source_type`, `start_time` and `end_time` for a template). Nothing is read from S3; the answer comes from the source's row counts in well under a second.

All timestamps are UTC; when `server_timezone` is not UTC, write each bound as toDateTime('<value>', 'UTC') rather than as a bare literal, which would be parsed in the server's timezone.

Every answer with a `decision` carries `notes`, what it says to do, written for this query: how to pass and merge its windows, what to replace before splitting a template that uses `{{time}}`, why the range could not be sized.

Returns `decision`:
- `run` — the range fits one call; run the query as written
- `windows` — Run the query once per window, newest first, with `dt >= '<from>' AND dt < '<to>'` in place of its time filter, and merge the results yourself: rows concatenate; `count()` and `sum()` add up; `min()` and `max()` combine; an average needs `sum()` and `count()` per window; `quantile(...)`, `uniq(...)`, `count(DISTINCT ...)` and `topK(...)` do not merge across windows, so keep those to one window or add filters. For a template whose time filter is `{{start_time}}`/`{{end_time}}`, pass each window as `start_time` = `from` and `end_time` = `to` instead. When `query` splits such a template itself (its description names the two shapes), `notes` says to call `query` once instead, and the windows are only a fallback. At most 200 windows are returned; `more_windows` counts the older ones the range still holds. More windows than you will run means the range needs rethinking: narrow the time filter, add filters on `raw` before extracting JSON, or set `sampling=` to `suggested_sampling` to estimate rather than measure. A window marked `oversized` holds more than the budget in a single second: add filters or `sampling=` for it
- `unsized` — the query's shape cannot be sized; `explanation` says what to change

With `run` or `windows`:
- `hot_tail` (never for a `{{source}}` template or a query that reads the hot collection itself with `remote()`) — the newest rows of the range are still in the hot collection, which `s3Cluster` holds only once they leave it: `from` is the oldest row still there (Live tail's first row on disk), `estimated_rows` how many of the range's rows that is, `collection` the hot collection to read them from when the row type names one; the top-level `estimated_rows` and the windows then count S3 rows only. Run the same query against `remote(<collection>)` with the time filter unchanged and no `_row_type` filter, and merge it in as one more window. The windows deliberately read past `from`, so a row uploaded to S3 since then is in both legs: add `AND dt < <from>` to them when the merged `count()` or `sum()` has to be exact. Without `from` the boundary could not be probed and the range merely reaches into the last hours
- `hot_rows` (a `{{source}}` template, or a query that reads the hot collection itself, whose range is over the budget with its hot rows counted) — how many rows of the range are still in the hot collection: the query reads them too, but `estimated_rows` and the budget leave them out, since a hot read is usually fast. Without `hot_rows`, `estimated_rows` counts them. If the query still times out on them, the timeout lists windows that split them
- `suggested_sampling` — with more windows than you will run, the `sampling=` rate at which the whole range fits one call

source_type.description: Required with `{{source}}`: which data `{{source}}` reads. `web_events` = browser/RUM events from the JS tag; `exceptions` = raw exception events of Errors sources (both queried like logs)

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__render_chart
tools.description:
Execute a ClickHouse SQL query and visualize the result as a chart.

Use `chart_type` to choose the visualization:
- `line` (default) — trends over time. Alias columns as `time`, `value`, and optional `series`.
- `bar` — magnitude over time or across buckets. Uses the same columns as `line`; set `stacked: true` to stack the series.
- `pie` — share of a total across categories. Alias a categorical column `AS series` (the slice label) and a numeric column `AS value` (the slice size), e.g. `SELECT service AS series, count() AS value FROM ... GROUP BY service`.

Write the query as a template and the server builds the collections for you, as Better Stack's dashboards and AI SRE do:
- `FROM {{source}}` reads the source's recent and historical rows of `source_type` together (for metrics, its metrics collection), scoped to the source
- `{{start_time}}` and `{{end_time}}` are the `start_time` and `end_time` arguments, e.g. `WHERE dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`
- `{{time}}` buckets `dt` to an interval that suits the range (`toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL '<n> second')`); `{{interval_seconds}}` is that interval
A template needs `source_type`, `start_time` and `end_time`, and no `table`. A query without `{{...}}` runs exactly as written, needs `table` and must name its `remote(...)` and `s3Cluster(...)` collections itself.

Alias result columns as (line/bar):
- `... AS time` — the time bucket (e.g., `{{time}} AS time` in a template, or `toStartOfHour(dt) AS time`)
- `... AS value` — the numeric metric (e.g., `count() AS value`)
- `... AS series` — optional: a grouping column for multiple series (e.g., `service AS series`)

**IMPORTANT (line/bar): Always choose a time granularity that produces 50–500 data points** (`{{time}}` picks 30 seconds to 2 hours from the range, which is in that band up to a day but gives more points on longer ranges: bucket by hand there) — too few points make the chart useless, too many make it unreadable. Use these rules based on the query's time range:
- Up to 1 hour → `toStartOfMinute(dt) AS time` → ~60 points
- 1–24 hours → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 5 MINUTE) AS time` → up to 288 points
- 1–7 days → `toStartOfHour(dt) AS time` → up to 168 points
- 7–30 days → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 4 HOUR) AS time` → up to 180 points
- 30–90 days → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 12 HOUR) AS time` → up to 180 points
- 90+ days → `toStartOfDay(dt) AS time`

Additional query instructions (data access patterns) are in:
- `query_help` — logs and spans
- `errors_query_help` — errors
- `metrics_query_help` — metrics

Before a query over more than a few hours of logs, spans or other events, call `query_windows` with the same arguments: it says whether the range fits one call and, if not, the time windows that do.

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__set_dashboard_variable
tools.description:
Create or update a dashboard template variable — a user-facing filter in the dashboard toolbar, referenced in chart SQL as `{{name}}` (required — the chart errors until it resolves to a value) or `[[ AND col = {{name}} ]]` (optional — the whole `[[ ... ]]` clause is dropped while the variable is empty).

Saving a chart auto-creates a plain text variable (or a source variable when the name contains 'source') for any undefined required `{{name}}`, but it starts empty — use this tool to give it a typed definition or a default value so the chart resolves without manual input.

Fields per type:
- `select_value` (shown as "Static list") → the options in `default_values` (first = default selection)
- `select_with_sql` (shown as "Dynamic list") → an option-yielding **expression** (NOT a full query) in `sql_definition`, e.g. `label('_host')`; see the `sql_definition` parameter for how it is interpolated
- Both list types accept `allow_multiple_values: true` to let users pick several options at once (interpolates as a regex used with `match()`). `multi_select_with_sql` is the legacy always-multiple Dynamic list; prefer `select_with_sql` with `allow_multiple_values: true`.
- `select_predefined_sql` (shown as "Query per value") → named SQL filters in `filters` (each a **full query**), default picked via `selected_label`
- `string` / `number` / `boolean` → `[default]` in `default_values`
- `sql_expression` → `[raw SQL]` in `default_values`, spliced into chart SQL unescaped
- `source` → the source IDs in `source_ids`. Name it `source` to set the dashboard's own source (which sources every chart queries by default), or use a custom name for an extra source variable that a chart references in its FROM (e.g. `FROM {{name}}`) to query a different set of sources than the dashboard default.
- `date` / `datetime` → an ISO date in `default_values`, e.g. `['2026-07-23']` or `['2026-07-23T14:30:00Z']`

SQL-backed types are validated at save time by running their SQL against the dashboard's source — the save is refused when it fails.

The names `start_time`, `end_time`, and `time` are reserved (they come from the time picker). `source` is the exception: set it as a source-type variable to change the dashboard's source. Use `dashboard` to list a dashboard's variables and `dashboard_query_help` for how each type is referenced in chart SQL.

allow_multiple_values.description: select_value / select_with_sql: let users pick several options at once; the variable then interpolates as a quoted regex used with `match()`, or as a parenthesised list when written straight after `IN` / `NOT IN`. Never `IN ({{var}})`, which keeps the regex and matches nothing. Ignored for other types.

default_values.description: select_value: the options (first = default). string/number/boolean: [default]. sql_expression: [raw SQL]. date/datetime: [ISO date], e.g. ['2026-07-23T14:30:00Z'].

filters.description: select_predefined_sql: named SQL filters. Unlike sql_definition, each sql is a FULL query returning one column, whose rows are injected into the chart as an IN-list. Filter time with `dt BETWEEN {{start_time}} AND {{end_time}}`, never {{time}} (that macro only buckets inside charts). Example: SELECT label('cmd') FROM {{source}} WHERE dt BETWEEN {{start_time}} AND {{end_time}} GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY count() DESC LIMIT 5.

name.description: Variable name used as {{name}} in chart queries

source_ids.description: source: the source IDs this variable resolves to (must be accessible to the dashboard's team). Ignored for other types.

sql_definition.description: select_with_sql / multi_select_with_sql: an expression (NOT a full query) yielding the option values — the platform interpolates it as `SELECT DISTINCT <sql_definition> AS option FROM {{source}} WHERE dt BETWEEN {{start_time}} AND {{end_time}} LIMIT 500` to populate the dropdown. Example: label('_host').

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__update_catalog_relation
tools.description:
Change a catalog relation: rename it, change its description or matching, add attributes or remove
them. Only what you pass changes. Removing an attribute removes its values from every record.
See `catalog_relations` for how the catalog works.

## Rules

- Name primary attributes after metadata keys incidents really carry. Check recent incidents' metadata with `incidents` and `incident` first: a key no incident carries never matches.
- Reference teams, team members, escalation policies and other Better Stack objects as objects, like `{"type": "Team", "name": "Platform"}`, never as their names in text.
- Never invent records. Every row comes from a source the user pointed you to (code, Terraform, Kubernetes, a Backstage catalog, the service map) or from the user.
- Prefer `upsert_catalog_records` to removing records and adding them again: it keeps every record it doesn't name, while removing them all empties the relation.

primary.description: true for a key column, named after a metadata key incidents carry. Defaults to false

match_mode.description: any = a record matches when one primary value matches, all = when every primary attribute does. Before switching to any, make sure no two records share a primary value

name.description: The relation's new name

relation_id.description: The ID of the catalog relation (from catalog_relations)

remove_attributes.description: Names of the attributes to remove, with their values

tools.risk_rationale: destructiveHint=true; changes a catalog relation's name/description/matching/attributes; removing an attribute removes its values from every record, a configuration overwrite with data-shape impact, medium.

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__upsert_catalog_records
tools.description:
Add or update a catalog relation's records, keyed by their primary values, so running the same sync
again updates instead of duplicating. A record whose primary values equal a row's is updated: the
added attributes the row names are replaced, the others are left alone. A row no record matches
becomes a new record. One invalid row fails the whole call and writes nothing. Up to 100
records per call. See `catalog_relations` for how the catalog works.

Name `Dependencies` and `Connections` by the other records' primary values.

## Rules

- Name primary attributes after metadata keys incidents really carry. Check recent incidents' metadata with `incidents` and `incident` first: a key no incident carries never matches.
- Reference teams, team members, escalation policies and other Better Stack objects as objects, like `{"type": "Team", "name": "Platform"}`, never as their names in text.
- Never invent records. Every row comes from a source the user pointed you to (code, Terraform, Kubernetes, a Backstage catalog, the service map) or from the user.
- Prefer `upsert_catalog_records` to removing records and adding them again: it keeps every record it doesn't name, while removing them all empties the relation.

records.description: Each record maps attribute names to values: text, an object like {"type": "Team", "name": "Platform"}, or a list of them; an empty list, null or blank text is an empty cell. Like [{"service": "checkout", "Owner": {"type": "Team", "name": "Payments"}, "Dependencies": ["payments-db"], "Type": "Backend"}]

relation_id.description: The ID of the catalog relation (from catalog_relations)

tools.risk_rationale: destructiveHint=true, idempotentHint=true; adds or updates catalog records (keyed by primary value, safe to re-run), a bulk data write that feeds incident metadata enrichment and escalation routing, medium.

Resolves a package/product name to a Context7-compatible library ID and returns matching libraries.

You MUST call this function before 'Query Documentation' tool to obtain a valid Context7-compatible library ID UNLESS the user explicitly provides a library ID in the format '/org/project' or '/org/project/version' in their query.

Each result includes:

- Name: Library or package name
- Description: Short summary
- Code Snippets: Number of available code examples
- Source Reputation: Authority indicator (High, Medium, Low, or Unknown)
- Benchmark Score: Quality indicator (100 is the highest score)
- Versions: List of versions if available. Use one of those versions if the user provides a version in their query. The format of the version is /org/project/version.

For best results, select libraries based on name match, source reputation, snippet coverage, benchmark score, and relevance to your use case.

Selection Process:
1. Analyze the query to understand what library/package the user is looking for
2. Return the most relevant match based on:
- Name similarity to the query (exact matches prioritized)
- Description relevance to the query's intent
- Documentation coverage (prioritize libraries with higher Code Snippet counts)
- Source reputation (consider libraries with High or Medium reputation more authoritative)
- Benchmark Score: Quality indicator (100 is the highest score)

- Return the selected library ID in a clearly marked section
- Provide a brief explanation for why this library was chosen
- If multiple good matches exist, acknowledge this but proceed with the most relevant one
- If no good matches exist, clearly state this and suggest query refinements

For ambiguous queries, request clarification before proceeding with a best-guess match.

Extracts all citations locally using eyecite, then verifies each
unique case citation against CourtListener's database via the
citation-lookup API. Returns case name, date, citation count,
and verification status for each citation.

* **unique case cluster** — distinct CourtListener case clusters

Three locations: title + part + section for one section; title + part alone for the whole part, with its Authority and Source notes, an index of its sections, and the names of its appendices; title + appendix for one appendix, passing the identifier exactly as regulations_browse_cfr emits it. A section can be written as people cite it — "61", "§ 141.61", "141.61(c)", or the full cite "40 CFR 141.61" in part 141 all read 40 CFR 141.61 — and a part as "Part 141"; the response names the identifier it read. Text comes back as a window of up to 64,000 characters (max_chars raises it to 200,000) with the total length and, when text remains, the offset to resume from; whole parts run to millions of characters, so page with offset or read a single section. eCFR retains historical versions from 2017 through the title's up-to-date date; a date outside that window is rejected with the window named. Current single-section reads are served from a synced local mirror when it holds the title's latest eCFR issue; the source is reported.

anyOf.description: Appendix identifier (e.g. "Appendix A-1 to Part 50").

appendix.description: Appendix identifier, verbatim as eCFR writes it — the `appendix` field or the leading phrase of the `cfrCite` on a regulations_browse_cfr appendix node or search hit. It is free-form prose, not a letter: "Appendix A-1 to Part 50", "Appendix A to Subpart C of Part 4", "Schedule I to Part 789", "Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88". Pass the whole phrase; a short form such as "A-1" matches nothing. Cannot be combined with section.

anyOf.description: ISO 8601 date (YYYY-MM-DD).

date.description: Point-in-time date, ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD). Default current. eCFR serves 2017-01-01 through the title's up-to-date date, usually a few days behind today; a date outside that window is rejected, naming the window.

max_chars.description: Most text characters to return in this window (1–200,000, default 64,000).

offset.description: Character offset into the text where the window starts (default 0). Pass bodyTextNextOffset from the previous call to read on, or a sections[].offset from a whole-part read to jump to that section.

part.description: CFR part within the title (e.g. "50"). Parts can be alphanumeric; a leading "Part" or "Pt." is dropped ("Part 141" reads part 141). Required unless appendix is given, where it is optional but recommended: an appendix identifier is unique within a part, not within a title, so without a part eCFR picks one of the matches. Obtain from regulations_browse_cfr or a Federal Register document's cfrReferences.

anyOf.description: Section identifier (e.g. "50.1").

section.description: Section within the part, normally written part.section as eCFR identifies it ("141.61"). Also accepted: the number alone ("61" in part 141), a leading "§" or "Sec.", a paragraph cite ("141.61(c)"), which reads the whole section, and the full cite this tool returns as cfrCite ("40 CFR 141.61", "14 CFR 241 § 25"), whose title has to match title. Identifiers eCFR writes differently are read as given — 14 CFR 241 numbers its sections "25" and "1-1". Omit to fetch the entire part. Cannot be combined with appendix.

title.description: CFR title number (1–50). E.g. 40 for "Protection of Environment".

tools.risk_rationale: Upstream advertises readOnlyHint=true, and the description and input schema expose no mutation, deletion, publication or external-message effect. The tool name was also checked against a mutation-verb list and contains none.

tools.name: federal-regulations__regulations_get_docket
tools.description: Pull a rulemaking docket from Regulations.gov by docket ID (e.g. "EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-0194") — the docket's metadata (title, agency, RIN, abstract) and the documents filed in it (NPRM, final rule, supporting materials). The docket is the folder holding a rule's whole paper trail; each returned document's objectId feeds regulations_find_comments. A docket often contains hundreds of supporting materials — filter document_types to "Proposed Rule"/"Rule" to find the rule documents themselves. Requires REGULATIONS_GOV_API_KEY (free at https://api.data.gov/signup/); the Federal Register and eCFR tools work without it.

docket_id.description: Regulations.gov docket ID (e.g. "EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-0194"). Obtain from regulationsGovDocketId on a regulations_search_rules or regulations_list_open_comments row, or docketId from regulations_get_document. The printed docketIds on those tools are not always Regulations.gov IDs ("REG-101355-26" is the IRS's own number for docket IRS-2026-0925).

document_types.description: Filter the docket's documents to these types. Omit for all. A docket often contains hundreds of "Supporting & Related Material" items — filter to "Proposed Rule"/"Rule" to find the rule documents.

page.description: Page number (1–40, default 1). Regulations.gov serves 40 pages, so a docket listing reaches 40 × per_page documents (10,000 at per_page 250); totalPages and nextPage in the response say how far this one goes. Beyond that, narrow with document_types.

per_page.description: Documents per page (5–250, default 25). Regulations.gov requires a minimum page size of 5.

tools.risk_rationale: Upstream advertises readOnlyHint=true, and the description and input schema expose no mutation, deletion, publication or external-message effect. The tool name was also checked against a mutation-verb list and contains none.

tools.name: federal-regulations__regulations_get_document
tools.description: Fetch one Federal Register document by its FR document number — full metadata (title, type, agencies, abstract, action, effective/comment dates, RINs) plus the cross-source handles that make this a workflow server. The output carries the Regulations.gov docket ID (chain into regulations_get_docket or regulations_find_comments), the docket numbers the Federal Register prints (chain back into regulations_search_rules as docket_id), the comment count and comment URL, and the affected CFR parts (chain into regulations_get_cfr_section). Set include_full_text only when the rule body itself is needed: it returns the plain-text body as a window of up to 64,000 characters (max_chars raises it to 200,000), with the body's total length and, when text remains, the offset to resume from. Short documents return whole; major final rules run past a million characters, so page through with offset rather than reading them in one call.

document_number.description: Federal Register document number, as regulations_search_rules returns it in documentNumber: "2024-07773" from 2010 on, older and correction numbers like "98-1572", "E9-25990", or "C1-2009-30484".

include_full_text.description: When true, inline one window of the document body as plain text (see offset and max_chars). Omitted, the body URLs alone come back unless offset or max_chars is passed; fetch full text only when you need to read the rule itself, not just its metadata and cross-links.

max_chars.description: Most body characters to return in this window (1–200,000, default 64,000). Implies include_full_text.

offset.description: Character offset into the plain-text body where the window starts (default 0). Pass the fullTextNextOffset from the previous call to read on. Implies include_full_text.

tools.risk_rationale: Upstream advertises readOnlyHint=true, and the description and input schema expose no mutation, deletion, publication or external-message effect. The tool name was also checked against a mutation-verb list and contains none.

tools.name: federal-regulations__regulations_list_open_comments
tools.description: List Federal Register documents currently open for public comment, sorted by closing date (soonest first) across the whole open window, filterable by document type, agency slug, and topic. "What can I still weigh in on?" Covers proposed rules and the final rules that take comment (direct final and interim final rules) by default; add NOTICE for the much larger set of notices with comment periods. Runs on the Federal Register's open-comment window and needs no key: each row carries its Regulations.gov docket and document IDs, comment count, and comment URL from the Federal Register document's embedded Regulations.gov info. Open one row with regulations_get_document for the full document, or pull the comments with regulations_find_comments (which, like regulations_get_docket, needs REGULATIONS_GOV_API_KEY).

agencies.description: Filter to one or more agencies by Federal Register agency slug (e.g. "environmental-protection-agency") — lowercase kebab-case, not a name or acronym. Every row lists its agencies with their slugs; read agencies[].slug off a row here or in regulations_search_rules. One unrecognized slug fails the whole request.

anyOf.description: ISO 8601 date (YYYY-MM-DD).

closing_before.description: Only documents whose comment period closes on or before this date, ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD), a real calendar day. Use to find deadlines you need to act on soon.

page.description: Page number, default 1. Pages run over the whole open window in closing-date order; totalPages and nextPage in the response say how far it goes.

per_page.description: Documents per page (1–100, default 20).

query.description: Full-text filter across open documents. Omit to list every document currently open for comment.

type.description: Document types to include: PRORULE (proposed rules), RULE (final rules that request comment, including direct final and interim final rules), NOTICE (information-collection and other notices with comment periods — a much larger set). Default, and when empty: ["PRORULE", "RULE"].

tools.risk_rationale: Upstream advertises readOnlyHint=true, and the description and input schema expose no mutation, deletion, publication or external-message effect. The tool name was also checked against a mutation-verb list and contains none.

tools.name: federal-regulations__regulations_search_rules
tools.description: Search the Federal Register — the daily journal of US proposed rules, final rules, notices, and presidential documents (1994–present) — filtering by full-text query, document type, agency slug, publication date range, affected CFR title and part, printed docket number, and RIN, all combined. A page cite from a CFR source note ("89 FR 49102", with its date) resolves to the documents printed on that page. The primary discovery entry point: results carry the document number (open with regulations_get_document), its citation and page range, each issuing agency with its filterable slug, printed docket numbers, Regulations.gov docket and document IDs, comment count and comment URL, whether the comment period is open, RINs, and affected CFR parts that chain into the comment and codified-text tools. A query ranks by relevance unless order says otherwise; filter-only browsing lists newest first. The Federal Register caps navigation at 50 pages and the match count at 10,000; when a result set is larger, narrow with published_after/published_before rather than paging deeper.

agencies.description: Filter to one or more agencies by Federal Register agency slug (e.g. "environmental-protection-agency", "securities-and-exchange-commission") — lowercase kebab-case, not a name or acronym. Every result lists its agencies with their slugs; if unsure, search by query and read agencies[].slug off a result. One unrecognized slug fails the whole request.

cfr_part.description: Only documents whose cfrReferences list this part of cfr_title: a part number ("141") or a range ("140-143"), such as the part regulations_get_cfr_section just read; a "Part" or "pt." prefix is dropped. Requires cfr_title. A part with a letter in it ("1203a") cannot be filtered on. Unlike a query of "40 CFR 141", which matches documents that mention the part, this matches the documents whose CFR references list it.

cfr_title.description: Only documents whose affected CFR parts (cfrReferences) fall in this title (1–50) — such as the title regulations_get_cfr_section just read. Alone it filters to the title; with cfr_part, to that part.

anyOf.description: Federal Register volume and page, "89 FR 49102".

citation.description: A Federal Register page cite, "89 FR 49102" (volume FR page) — such as one from the source note that ends a regulations_get_cfr_section bodyText. Returns the documents printed on that page, usually one and sometimes a few sharing it, ordered by start page. Requires citation_date and replaces published_after/published_before. Volume 59 (1994) onward.

anyOf.description: ISO 8601 date (YYYY-MM-DD).

citation_date.description: The publication date printed beside the cite in the source note (YYYY-MM-DD) — "89 FR 49102, June 11, 2024" is 2024-06-11. Required with citation; its year is the volume + 1935.

docket_id.description: Only documents carrying this docket number as the Federal Register prints it — a docketIds entry from a result here or from regulations_get_document, with or without a wrapper such as "Docket No.". Lists a docket's Federal Register documents with no REGULATIONS_GOV_API_KEY. A Regulations.gov docket ID matches only where the Federal Register prints it. Pass the complete number: a fragment ("FAA-2026") matches every docket that contains it.

order.description: Result order. Defaults to relevance with a query, newest without one. relevance without a query falls back to newest first; oldest lists the earliest publications first. Ignored with citation, whose matches come in page order.

page.description: Page number (1–50, default 1). The Federal Register serves 50 pages, so a query reaches 50 × per_page matches (5,000 at per_page 100); totalPages and nextPage in the response say how far this one goes. To reach past that, narrow with published_after/published_before rather than paging deeper.

per_page.description: Results per page (2–100, default 20). The Federal Register API treats exactly 1 as its default page size instead of returning one result.

anyOf.description: ISO 8601 date (YYYY-MM-DD).

published_after.description: Earliest publication date, ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD), a real calendar day. Combine with published_before to window large result sets — the FR caps navigation at 50 pages.

anyOf.description: ISO 8601 date (YYYY-MM-DD).

published_before.description: Latest publication date, ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD), a real calendar day.

query.description: Full-text search across document title and body. Omit to browse by filters alone (e.g. all EPA proposed rules in a date range).

rin.description: Only documents carrying this Regulation Identifier Number — a regulationIdNumbers entry such as "2040-AG18", which follows one rulemaking from proposal to final rule. Pass the complete RIN: a fragment ("2040") matches every RIN that contains it.

type.description: Document types to include. PRORULE=Proposed Rule, RULE=Final Rule, NOTICE=Notice, PRESDOCU=Presidential Document. Omit for all types.
